Volume 13 · Chapter 03

Uncertainty and information

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c02

By the endAnalyze risk attitudes and the economic value of information formally.

Volume 13 · Chapter 3

Uncertainty and information

A forecast can be informative yet worthless for a particular decision. A less noisy experiment can be too expensive, and two experiments can each be indispensable for a different task. Before ranking them, specify what is uncertain, which actions remain available, how consequences are valued, and when information is acquired. This chapter derives the preference and information orders that make those statements precise.

Capability. Construct expected utility on finite lotteries; compare risks without confusing a variance statistic with a preference order; compute Bayesian decision values; and prove the finite Blackwell theorem in both directions. Six original worked cases and twelve solved exercises distinguish universal theorems from a single decision problem. All probabilities and payoffs in the cases are stipulated, synthetic inputs.

Prerequisites. Preference representation supplies weak orders and ordinal uniqueness; Consumer and producer duality supplies disciplined domains and optimization. Use finite expectation and conditional probability from Volume 3, Chapter 1, Jensen’s inequality and certainty equivalents from Chapter 10, and compactness and calculus from Volume 2, Chapter 10. The needed finite separation lemma is proved below, rather than assumed from a later equilibrium chapter.

1. Why lottery utility has a cardinal scale

Let C be a nonempty finite prize set and Δ(C) its probability simplex. A lottery p assigns probabilities pc≥0 summing to one; δc is the sure prize c. A compound lottery is reduced to its final prize probabilities. Thus αp+(1−α)q means a probability mixture, not a physical average of two prizes. Write ≽ for a complete, transitive preference on every lottery in Δ(C), with ∼ and ≻ denoting indifference and strict preference.

Mixture continuity requires, for every p,q,r, that both {α∈[0,1]:αp+(1−α)q≽r} and {α∈[0,1]:r≽αp+(1−α)q} are closed. Independence requires, for every p,q,r and 0<α≤1,

p≽q ⇔ αp+(1−α)r ≽ αq+(1−α)r.

The equivalence also preserves strict preference and indifference: apply it in both directions of a comparison. It says that adding the same probabilistic consequence to both alternatives does not reverse their order. It is a substantive behavioral restriction, not a consequence of transitivity.

Finite expected-utility theorem. These axioms hold if and only if some prize index u represents preference by U(p)=Σcpcu(c). Here is a construction covering ties and degenerate cases. Among the finitely many sure prizes choose a best b and a worst w by successive weak-order comparison. Replacing one lottery component at a time by b or w, using independence and reduction of mixtures, gives δb≽p≽δw for every p. Zero probability components may be omitted. If b∼w, transitivity makes every lottery indifferent; any constant u represents it.

Otherwise b≻w. Put L(t)=tδb+(1−t)δw. For t>0, independence gives L(t)≻δw. For t>s≥0, L(s)=(s/t)L(t)+(1−s/t)δw; mixing the strict comparison L(t)≻δw with the common lottery L(t) proves L(t)≻L(s). For a given p let A={t:L(t)≽p} and B={t:p≽L(t)}. These are closed, cover [0,1] by completeness, and contain 1 and 0 respectively. The minimum t* of the nonempty compact A belongs to B: if positive, every smaller t is outside A and hence in B, and closedness passes to the limit; if zero, membership is already known. Consequently L(t*)∼p, uniquely by the strict ordering of L.

Define U(p)=t*. Substituting the indifferent L(U(p)) and L(U(q)) into mixtures, one at a time using independence, gives

αp+(1−α)q ∼ L(αU(p)+(1−α)U(q)),
U(αp+(1−α)q)=αU(p)+(1−α)U(q).

Transitivity and the strict order of L prove that U represents ≽. Repeatedly decomposing p into sure prizes proves U(p)=ΣpcU(δc), so take u(c)=U(δc). This also shows tied prizes receive the same index. Conversely a finite linear expectation is continuous in mixture probabilities, complete and transitive through the real order, and independent because the common expected term cancels and α is positive.

Uniqueness. If another index v represents the same lottery preference and b≻w, then v(b)>v(w). Indifference δc∼L(u(c)) gives v(c)=v(w)+[v(b)−v(w)]u(c). Thus any two expected-utility indices differ by a positive affine transformation, and every such transformation preserves the order. If all prizes tie, both indices are constant; their scale is uninformative. General strictly increasing transformations preserve the ordering of sure prizes, but need not preserve expected-utility comparisons.

Worked case 1: calibration and an observable independence failure

Three abstract prizes L,M,H satisfy H≻M≻L and M∼(3/10)H+(7/10)L. Normalize u(L)=0 and u(H)=1, so u(M)=3/10. Lotteries A and B have probability vectors (1/5,1/2,3/10) and (0,3/4,1/4) in that order. Their expected utilities are (9/20,19/40), hence B≻A. The index 2u+5 gives (59/10,119/20), preserving the order. Squaring the prize index gives (69/200,127/400), now ranking A higher. Squaring is strictly increasing on {0,3/10,1}; its failure concerns lotteries, not the order of sure prizes.

For a separate example on monetary prizes {0,2,4,10}, define V(p)=Ep[X]−Varp(X)/4. Comparing this polynomial gives a complete, transitive and mixture-continuous preference. Let P be sure 2, Q give 0 with probability 2/5 and 4 with probability 3/5, and R be sure 10. Then V(P)=2 and V(Q)=12/5−(96/25)/4=36/25, so P≻Q. But V((P+R)/2)=6−16/4=2, while V((Q+R)/2)=31/5−(409/25)/4=211/100. The four values are (2,36/25,2,211/100). Adding the same half-chance of 10 reverses the preference. Therefore this entire lottery preference has no expected-utility representation; it is not merely a poor choice of utility normalization. No monotonicity over all lotteries is asserted for V.

The finite lottery axioms and representation scope are supported by MIT’s 2015 risk notes, printed pages 7–14. The construction and both numerical examples above are original.

2. Risk attitudes, certainty equivalents and local approximations

We now assume an expected-utility representation u on a wealth interval I for every finite-support lottery considered. The finite-prize theorem alone does not construct this continuum representation. Suppose u is continuous and strictly increasing. For finite X supported in I, its mean μ lies in I, and E[u(X)] lies between the utility of its smallest and largest possible wealth. The intermediate-value theorem and strict monotonicity give a unique certainty equivalent CEu(X)=u−1(E[u(X)]) in that range. The risk premium is ρu(X)=μ−CEu(X), in wealth units. Without strict monotonicity the inverse and uniqueness need not exist.

Concavity of u implies u(μ)≥E[u(X)] by finite Jensen, hence ρ≥0. Conversely, preferring the mean of every two-point lottery gives u(αx+(1−α)y)≥αu(x)+(1−α)u(y), exactly concavity. Thus this risk-aversion condition on all finite lotteries is equivalent to concavity. Strict concavity makes the premium strictly positive for every nondegenerate lottery; weak concavity alone allows zero premia on affine portions. Affine utility gives zero premium for every lottery. These are statements about the expected-utility index, whose admissible affine changes preserve them.

Comparative risk aversion. Let u,v be C² on the same connected open interval I, with u′,v′>0. Define absolute risk aversion Au(x)=−u″(x)/u′(x). For φ=v∘u−1, the chain rule gives

φ′(u(x))=v′(x)/u′(x)>0,
φ″(u(x)) = [v′(x)/(u′(x))²][Au(x)−Av(x)].

Consequently Av≥Au everywhere if and only if φ is concave. Jensen applied to φ then gives E[v(X)]≤φ(E[u(X)])=v(CEu(X)), so CEv(X)≤CEu(X) for every finite X. Conversely, that certainty-equivalent order for every binary lottery, followed by applying increasing v, gives Jensen’s inequality for φ on u(I); hence φ is concave and the derivative inequality follows. The equivalence compares all supported risks on this common interval, not just the lottery in one example. Positive affine changes leave A unchanged. A has units inverse to wealth; xA(x) is the dimensionless relative index for positive wealth.

A local formula with a remainder. Let Xε=w+εZ, where Z is a fixed bounded finite-support variable with E[Z]=0. Suppose u is C³ on a compact neighborhood of w inside I and u′(w)>0. For sufficiently small |ε| every outcome stays in that neighborhood. Taylor’s theorem, with a uniform bound on |u‴|, gives E[u(Xε)]=u(w)+u″(w)ε²E[Z²]/2+O(|ε|³). Continuity makes CE approach w; on a smaller neighborhood u′ is bounded away from zero. The mean-value theorem first yields CE−w=O(ε²). Taylor expanding u(CE) there now gives

ρu(Xε) = ½Au(w)ε²Var(Z)+O(|ε|³).

The bound depends on the fixed shock, derivative bounds and neighborhood. It is not an exact formula for arbitrary large risk, and a sequence of unbounded shocks is outside these hypotheses.

Worked case 2: the same wealth risk under two utilities

Wealth is 7 or 13 with equal probability, so its mean is 10. For u(x)=log x on (0,∞), CE=√91 and ρ=10−√91, approximately 0.460608. For v(x)=−1/x, E[v]=−10/91, CE=91/10 and ρ=9/10. Here Au=1/x and Av=2/x; also φ(t)=−exp(−t) is increasing and strictly concave. The higher reciprocal-utility premium follows both directly and from the comparison theorem.

For the smaller family 10±3ε, |ε|<10/3, the log certainty equivalent is exactly √(100−9ε²). The local premium is 9ε²/20. At ε=1 it gives 9/20, below the exact premium. Rationalizing the square root twice gives the exact approximation error

10−√(100−9ε²)−9ε²/20 = 81ε⁴ / {20[10+√(100−9ε²)]²}.

At ε=1/2, CE=√391/2 and the local premium is 9/80. Since √391/2>9, the positive error is less than 81/115520, which is less than 1/1000; its actual value is approximately 0.000640. This is numerical evidence for this explicit risk, with an analytic bound, rather than an assertion that second-order approximations are always adequate.

MIT’s risk-attitude notes, printed pages 19–23 support the concavity and comparative-risk-aversion concepts. The local remainder and exact error calculation are derived here.

3. Orders over distributions and the role of equal means

Let X,Y have finite supports in a common bounded interval [a,b]. Write FX(t)=Pr(X≤t). First-order stochastic dominance, X≽₁Y, means E[u(X)]≥E[u(Y)] for every weakly increasing real utility u on that interval. It is equivalent to FX(t)≤FY(t) for every real t. This definition includes constant utilities and ties; dominance does not promise a strict gain for every utility.

For a complete finite proof, take the union of support points x₁<⋯<xm, giving either distribution zero mass where necessary. If m=1 the claim is immediate. Otherwise summation by parts gives

E[u(X)]−E[u(Y)] = Σk=1m−1[u(xk+1)−u(xk)][FY(xk)−FX(xk)].

One way to verify the identity is to write u(xj)=u(x₁)+Σk<j[u(xk+1)−u(xk)] and interchange the finite sums. Nonnegative increments prove sufficiency. Necessity follows by testing each increasing indicator u(x)=1{x>xk}. CDFs are constant between these points, so no untested thresholds remain. If at least one CDF inequality is strict, every strictly increasing utility gives a strict expected gain.

Second-order dominance, here meaning the increasing-concave order X≽₂Y, requires the same expected inequality for every weakly increasing concave u. Put LX(t)=E[(t−X)+], where z+=max(z,0). For t≥a, LX(t)=∫atFX(s)ds, including when there is an atom at a. The equivalent condition is

X≽₂Y ⇔ LX(t)≤LY(t) for every real t.

Necessity uses the increasing concave test ut(x)=−(t−x)+. For sufficiency, thresholds t≥b imply E[X]≥E[Y]. Interpolate any concave increasing u linearly between union support points. Its successive slopes d₁≥⋯≥dm−1≥0, and on that support its value equals

u(xm)+dm−1(x−xm)−Σj=2m−1(dj−1−dj)(xj−x)+.

Each hinge coefficient is nonnegative. The mean and L inequalities therefore give the desired expectation order. For two support points the hinge sum is empty; for one it is trivial. Differences of the L functions are linear between union knots, zero below both supports, and constant above both supports. Thus checking those finitely many knots verifies the condition for all real thresholds. No density or differentiability assumption is needed.

A mean-preserving spread is a joint construction of X,Y with their specified marginals and E[Y|X]=X. Conditional Jensen yields E[u(Y)|X]≤u(X) for concave u, and expectation gives X≽₂Y; also E[Y]=E[X]. Equal means are part of the spread concept, but not part of our increasing-concave dominance definition. For finite supports the converse is also true: equal means together with X≽₂Y imply such a coupling. The next argument proves existence rather than silently invoking a coupling theorem.

Finite separation lemma. For a nonempty compact convex set K⊂ℝd and z∉K, choose a nearest point c, which exists by compactness. Set h=z−c. For k∈K, the segment c+t(k−c) stays in K for 0≤t≤1. The squared distance to z is minimized at t=0, so its right derivative gives h·(k−c)≤0. Thus h·z=h·c+‖h‖²>maxk∈Kh·k. This is the only separating-hyperplane result needed here and in Section 5.

Finite spread converse. Let the positive-probability X atoms be xi with probabilities pi, and the Y atoms yj with probabilities qj. Their means agree. The increasing concave utility min(x,min y) rules out X mass below min y. The utility min(x,max y), together with equal means, rules out mass above max y. If Y is constant this forces X to be that constant and the coupling is immediate. Otherwise each xi lies in the Y interval, so there are conditional weights wij≥0 with Σjwij=1 and Σjwijyj=xi, using just the endpoints if necessary. Let K be the set of column marginals rj=Σipiwij attainable this way. It is a nonempty compact convex image of the product of these constrained simplices.

If q∉K, the lemma gives coefficients hj with h·q>maxr∈Kh·r. Define H(x)=max{Σjwjhj:w≥0,Σw=1,Σw y=x} on [min y,max y]. Maxima exist. Mixing feasible weights proves H is concave, and H(yj)≥hj. It is a finite piecewise-affine upper boundary with bounded slopes: at any optimum with at least three positive weights, a nonzero perturbation preserving mass and mean exists; optimality forces its objective slope to zero, so move until one weight vanishes, and repeat. The remaining candidates use at most two of the finitely many y points. Their finitely many line segments give the claimed shape; at either endpoint all weight concentrates there, so continuity also holds there. Choose a finite M making H(x)+Mx increasing. Equal means and X≽₂Y imply E[H(X)]≥E[H(Y)]≥h·q. Yet independent choice of each conditional row gives maxr∈Kh·r=ΣpiH(xi)=E[H(X)], a contradiction. Hence q∈K, and γij=piwij is the required joint law. This proof is finite; no arbitrary-support extension is claimed.

Worked case 3: a shift, a spread and a variance trap

First let A take 2,5 equally and B take 1,4 equally. At the union knots (1,2,4,5), FA−FB is (-1/2,0,-1/2,0), so A≽₁B and therefore A≽₂B. Their means are 7/2 and 5/2: this comparison is not a mean-preserving spread. Next compare sure 3 with equal chances of 1 and 5. Add conditional mean-zero noise ±2 to sure 3 to obtain the latter. Thus sure 3 dominates in the increasing-concave order, but the CDFs cross, so there is no first-order dominance. The utility min(x,3) values them at 3 and 2, while linear utility gives both value 3.

Finally let X take 0 with probability 1/3 and 3 with probability 2/3, while Y takes 1 with probability 3/4 and 5 with probability 1/4. Both means are 2; their variances are (2,3). At knots (0,1,3,5), their CDF differences are (1/3,-5/12,1/4,0), and their lower-partial-moment differences LX−LY are (0,1/3,-1/2,0). Both signs occur, so neither dominance order ranks them.

The preference witnesses are explicit: u(x)=min(x,1) gives expected values (2/3,1), preferring Y; v(x)=min(x,3) gives (2,3/2), preferring X. Both utilities are increasing and concave in the weak sense. Adding εx, ε>0, makes them strictly increasing without changing either ranking, since the means coincide. The lower variance of X is not a universal risk-averse preference certificate.

MIT’s dominance notes, printed pages 29–33 motivate these orders. Our finite summation, hinge and coupling arguments handle atoms directly and keep all-real-threshold quantifiers explicit. They do not rely on the source’s continuous-CDF proof restriction or its abbreviated spread-converse statement.

4. The value of a signal is a decision value

There are n finite states i, a prior πi≥0 summing to one, m signals s, and k feasible actions a. An experiment P is an n×m row-stochastic matrix: Pis=Pr(s|i), each row nonnegative and summing to one. The matrix Uia gives cardinal payoff utility in state i from action a; if it records money directly we assume risk neutrality over that money. The action is chosen after the signal. The signal probability qs=ΣiπiPis and, for qs>0, posterior βi(s)=πiPis/qs obey Σs:q_s>0qsβ(s)=π. A zero-probability signal has no defined Bayes posterior and contributes zero to value; assigning it an arbitrary posterior must not change the answer.

V(P,π,U)=ΣsmaxaΣiπiPisUia,
V₀(π,U)=maxaΣiπiUia,
V*(π,U)=ΣiπimaxaUia.

Because the action menu is unchanged, the decision maker can ignore the signal and choose an optimal prior action at every signal; hence V≥V₀. Allowing the action to vary by state gives V*, and each signal term is at most the sum of its statewise maxima, so V≤V*. Randomized actions cannot improve these values: at a given posterior, their expected payoff is an average of deterministic-action payoffs and cannot exceed the largest.

Exactly when is the gain strict? The gain is zero if and only if there is one action optimal at every positive-probability posterior. Such a common action attains V and, by averaging, V₀. Conversely choose a prior-optimal a*. The gain equals Σs:q_s>0qs[maxaβ(s)·Ua−β(s)·Ua*], a sum of nonnegative terms. If it is zero, each term vanishes, so a* is the required common action. Switching among tied optimal actions does not itself establish strict value.

An acquisition fee changes the comparison. Subtracting a monetary fee c directly from V is justified here only with risk-neutral money payoffs or an explicitly specified additive utility cost. With concave wealth utility, calculate E[u(w+payoff−c)] using the actual timing and resources; there is no general permission to subtract c from utility. Likewise an action commitment made before the signal, a prohibited randomization, or a changed menu is a different decision problem.

Worked case 4: a useful signal and a useless informative signal

States H,L have prior (1/3,2/3). Signals +,− have experiment P=((3/4,1/4),(1/4,3/4)), with states as rows. Investing yields risk-neutral money (6,−3) in H,L; the safe action yields (0,0). Without information both actions have value 0. Signal probabilities are (5/12,7/12) and posterior probabilities of H are (3/5,1/7). Investing then has conditional expected payoffs (12/5,-12/7). Invest after + and choose safe after −; V(P)=1, while perfect information has value 2. The gain over no information is 1.

A nonnegative certain fee c makes this experiment weakly preferable to no information exactly when c≤1, with indifference at 1. Now change only the investment payoff to (6,0). Investment is optimal at both posteriors, so information has no decision value: V(P)=V₀=2 despite the distinct posteriors. The experiment’s informativeness and the usefulness of its information for a specified action menu are different statements.

5. Blackwell dominance: simulation and its finite converse

Fix the same n states. Let P have m signals and Q have ℓ signals. A garbling is an m×ℓ row-stochastic matrix G with Q=PG. First observe s from P, then draw t according to Gst, using randomization conditionally independent of the state given s. The resulting state-conditional distribution of t is Q. This is a restriction on the whole experiment, not on one posterior variance or one forecast score.

Sufficiency. For any finite action set and payoff matrix U, a randomized rule D under Q is an ℓ×k row-stochastic matrix. Under P, use the feasible rule GD. Its state-by-action distribution is PGD=QD, so it gives the same expected payoff under every prior. Maximizing under P can do at least as well. Since deterministic posterior maximization is at least as good as any randomized rule, this proves V(P,π,U)≥V(Q,π,U) for every π,U. The free randomization and the unchanged action set are explicit parts of the argument.

Finite Blackwell theorem. P can garble into Q if and only if that value inequality holds for every finite decision problem and prior. To prove the nontrivial direction, consider K={PG:G is m×ℓ row-stochastic}, a nonempty compact convex set of n×ℓ matrices: products of finite closed simplices are compact and convex, and multiplication by fixed P is linear and continuous. If Q∉K, the separation lemma supplies H with

⟨H,Q⟩ > maxZ∈K⟨H,Z⟩, where ⟨H,Z⟩=Σi,tHitZit.

Take a uniform prior 1/n and ℓ actions labeled by Q’s signals, with payoff Uit=nHit. Under P, every randomized rule is an m×ℓ row-stochastic G, so the optimal value is maxZ∈K⟨H,Z⟩. Under Q, the feasible identity rule “take action t after signal t” earns ⟨H,Q⟩. Therefore V(Q)>V(P), contradicting the hypothesized order. The separator is not just an abstract certificate: after rescaling it is a decision problem witnessing the failure. If desired add the same constant to every payoff to make all nonnegative; all values shift equally and the strict comparison remains.

In fact, one fixed full-support prior suffices when the inequality is tested for every payoff matrix: replace nHit by Hit/πi. Full support is essential. With prior (1,0), the uninformative P=((1),(1)) and fully revealing Q=I₂ have equal values for every U, because the state is already known; but PG has identical rows for every G and cannot equal I₂. One decision problem, one accuracy statistic, and one prior lacking full support are each insufficient tests of the full experiment order.

The conditional-posterior picture is consistent with the algebra. In a garbled joint construction, the posterior given Q’s signal is the conditional average of the P posterior given that signal. This follows by summing πiPisGst over s and normalizing for positive signal probabilities. A coarser posterior can therefore discard decision-relevant distinctions. This observation alone does not replace the proved matrix equivalence.

Worked case 5: a real garbling, an impossible reverse and a price

Use P and the investment problem from case 4. Let G=((2/3,1/3),(1/3,2/3)), so the signal label is flipped with probability 1/3. Multiplication gives Q=((7/12,5/12),(5/12,7/12)). Under prior (1/3,2/3), Q’s signal probabilities are (17/36,19/36), and its H posteriors are (7/17,5/19). Investment is optimal only after its + signal; its conditional payoffs are (12/17,−12/19). Thus V(Q)=1/3, below V(P)=1.

Under P, simulate this Q policy by investing with probability 2/3 after + and 1/3 after −. Its state-conditional action probabilities equal those under Q, so its value is exactly 1/3; direct optimal use of P earns 1. Conversely Q is invertible and its only possible reverse matrix is Q⁻¹P=((2,-1),(-1,2)). The negative entries prevent a stochastic reverse garbling.

If P costs 3/4 and Q is free, P’s net value is 1/4, below 1/3. The maximal extra fee for preferring P to Q is V(P)−V(Q)=2/3. This does not refute Blackwell dominance: its comparison concerns free access to the experiments under identical payoff possibilities.

The row convention and finite decision comparison are supported by Börgers’s 3 December 2023 notes, pages 1–7. The proof here uses the explicitly proved nearest-point separation lemma; it does not ask the reader to accept an unproved minimax interchange.

6. Noncomparability and the evidence a ranking would need

Worked case 6: two tasks, opposite winners

There are three equally likely states. Experiment E=((1,0),(0,1),(0,1)) reports whether the state is 1. Experiment H=((0,1),(1,0),(0,1)) reports whether it is 2. In job 1, the two actions answer “state 1” or “not state 1,” receiving 1 for a correct answer and 0 otherwise. E has value 1, while H has value 2/3: after H’s second signal, states 1 and 3 are equally likely and either answer is correct with probability 1/2. Job 2 instead asks whether the state is 2, reversing the values. The ordered pairs (E,H) for the two jobs are ((1,2/3),(2/3,1)).

These witnesses rule out dominance in either direction. A direct matrix argument agrees: E’s rows 2 and 3 are equal, so those rows remain equal in every EG, whereas H’s are different. H’s rows 1 and 3 are equal, which similarly prevents garbling it into E. With the three actions “guess state i” and a payoff of 1 for a correct state, both experiments instead have value (2/3,2/3). Equality on that task does not make the experiments equivalent.

Both have signal probabilities (1/3,2/3). E’s posteriors are (1,0,0) and (0,1/2,1/2); H’s are (0,1,0) and (1/2,0,1/2). With π=(1/3,1/3,1/3), the statistic E[‖β−π‖²] equals (1/3)(2/3)+(2/3)(1/6)=1/3 for both. Equal posterior dispersion in this scalar sense also fails to establish a Blackwell relation. Which distinctions the signal resolves matters.

A research claim to audit. A report estimates two signal matrices, evaluates one prediction score, and recommends the higher-scoring system to every user. A formal universal claim requires a common state space and either a valid nonnegative row-stochastic G with Q=PG or value inequalities for the full stated class of decision problems. Case 6 disproves inference from one task or one dispersion score alone. A finite exact garbling is a model implication conditional on its supplied probabilities; it does not supply sampling uncertainty, stable measurement, transport to a new population, or truthful reporting by strategic agents.

For a practical recommendation, state the user’s prior, actions, timing, utility over consequences, acquisition and implementation costs, and rights to ignore or randomize. A risk-averse user’s money payoffs must be converted to utility using the declared wealth domain. A signal may alter available actions or reveal information to a rival, violating the fixed-menu single-decision framework. Those are reasons to change the model, not reasons to reverse the theorem’s inequality while retaining its assumptions.

7. Exercises

Unless a prompt explicitly asks for an approximation, use exact probabilities and fractions. Give hypotheses before applying a theorem. The proof questions concern all objects in the stated finite domain, not only a numerical grid.

  1. Representation and scale. Prove the finite expected-utility theorem from completeness, transitivity, mixture continuity and independence, including the all-indifferent case and uniqueness. In case 1, calculate both lottery values under u, 2u+5 and u²; explain the different invariance claims.
  2. An axiom under stress. Recompute the means, variances and V values of P,Q,(P+R)/2,(Q+R)/2 in case 1. Which of completeness, transitivity, mixture continuity and independence does the specified V preference violate? Explain why changing utility units cannot rescue an expected-utility representation.
  3. Global comparative risk aversion. Compute the two certainty equivalents and risk premiums for wealth 7 or 13. Derive the φ″ identity and the equivalence between Av≥Au and the certainty-equivalent order for every finite risk on a common interval. State all derivative and domain conditions.
  4. Approximation with control. Derive the local small-risk formula with an O(|ε|³) remainder under the stated hypotheses. For equal wealth probabilities on 10±3ε, derive the exact error identity and prove that at ε=1/2 the quadratic log-premium error is positive and less than 1/1000.
  5. First-order order. Derive the finite summation identity and prove both FSD directions. Apply it to equal-probability A=(2,5), B=(1,4), including union-support zero masses, strictness and why this pair cannot be a mean-preserving spread.
  6. Second-order order and coupling. Prove the lower-partial-moment characterization for finite supports. Show that a conditional-mean coupling gives equal means and the order. Prove the finite equal-mean converse using the separation lemma and H construction, including support bounds and why H can be made increasing by adding Mx. Illustrate with sure 3 versus equal chances of 1 and 5.
  7. A variance claim. A colleague claims every increasing concave utility prefers X=(0,3) with probabilities (1/3,2/3) to Y=(1,5) with probabilities (3/4,1/4), because both have mean 2 and X has smaller variance. Compute the CDF and L differences at all union knots and give two opposing increasing concave utility witnesses. Can the witnesses be made strictly increasing?
  8. Bayes and strict value. Derive all case-4 posteriors and optimal values, including the perfect-information bound and fee threshold. Prove the common-optimal-action characterization of zero value. Apply it when investment’s payoffs become (6,0), and explain why direct subtraction of a money fee is not valid for an arbitrary concave wealth utility.
  9. Garbling and acquisition. Compute Q=PG, its posteriors and value in case 5. Give the P decision rule simulating Q’s optimum. Prove reverse garbling is impossible, then compare a 3/4 fee for P with free Q and derive the exact extra-fee boundary.
  10. The converse, not just simulation. Prove both directions of the finite Blackwell theorem using the nearest-point separator. Turn a separator into an explicit payoff matrix and show why a fixed full-support prior suffices if every payoff matrix is tested. Give a prior without full support for which the same implication fails.
  11. Signals that cannot be ranked. For E,H in case 6, solve both binary tasks and three-state classification. Compute both posterior-energy statistics. Prove noncomparability both by task payoffs and by repeated rows. Identify the precise failed inference from equal classification performance or equal energy.
  12. Referee transfer, 12 points. A report says: “Our estimated signal has the highest classification accuracy and posterior dispersion. Therefore it Blackwell-dominates its rival, and every user should buy it at its posted fee, whatever their risk attitude. Our point estimate proves this population conclusion.” Write a corrected recommendation and an evidence plan. Address experiment ordering, task/prior/action specification, utility and risk, fees/timing/constraints, estimation and transport, and one informative counterexample or new test. State what would earn full credit in each dimension.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. Finite comparison supplies best and worst sure prizes. Independence permits replacing components one at a time, bounding every lottery between them. If they tie, every lottery ties and a constant index works. Otherwise L(t)=tb+(1−t)w is strictly ordered: L(t)≻w for t>0 by independence; mixing that comparison with L(t) proves L(t)≻L(s) when t>s. The closed cuts {t:L(t)≽p} and {t:p≽L(t)} cover [0,1] and include opposite endpoints. The minimum of the first lies in the second by a left-limit argument, yielding a unique indifference probability U(p). Transitivity makes U represent the order. Independence substitutes indifferent calibrated lotteries in any mixture, and reduction gives U(αp+(1−α)q)=αU(p)+(1−α)U(q). Decompose p into degenerate prizes to obtain expected utility. Linear expected utility conversely satisfies each axiom.

    For a second representing index v, calibration gives v(c)=v(w)+[v(b)−v(w)]u(c), with strictly positive slope when b≻w; tied prizes have equal labels. In the all-indifferent case both indices are constant. The numerical pairs are (9/20,19/40), (59/10,119/20), and (69/200,127/400). The first two rank B higher; the last ranks A higher because 138/400>127/400. Squaring preserves the three sure-prize comparisons but not the lottery comparison, whereas a positive affine map preserves every expected comparison.

  2. P has mean 2, variance 0 and V=2. Q has mean 12/5 and second moment 48/5, hence variance 48/5−144/25=96/25 and V=36/25. The P mixture has outcomes 2,10 equally, mean 6, variance 16 and V=2. The Q mixture has probabilities (1/5,3/10,1/2) at (0,4,10), mean 31/5 and second moment 274/5; its variance is 274/5−961/25=409/25 and V=211/100. Thus P is strictly preferred to Q but their common-R half-mixtures reverse that order. Comparisons through a real-valued polynomial are complete, transitive and mixture-continuous, so independence is the failing axiom. Any expected-utility representation would satisfy independence as an ordering property. Relabeling values cannot remove the observed reversal while representing that same ordering.

  3. Mean wealth is 10. Log expected utility is (log 7+log 13)/2=log√91, giving CE=√91 and premium 10−√91. Reciprocal utility has expectation −(1/7+1/13)/2=−10/91, giving CE=91/10 and premium 9/10. Both utilities are continuous, strictly increasing and strictly concave on (0,∞). Their absolute indices are 1/x and 2/x, and φ(t)=−e−t is increasing concave.

    On a common connected open interval with u,v∈C² and u′,v′>0, differentiate φ=v∘u−1 twice to get φ″(u(x))=(v′/(u′)²)(Au−Av). Thus the index order is equivalent to concavity of φ. Jensen implies E[v(X)]≤v(CEu), and increasing v yields CEv≤CEu. Conversely that CE inequality for every two-point X implies φ(αu(x)+(1−α)u(y))≥αφ(u(x))+(1−α)φ(u(y)); hence φ is concave on u(I) and the index order follows. Positive affine changes cancel in −u″/u′ and preserve the CE equation. Derivatives vanishing, incomparable domains, or a single tested lottery do not establish the full equivalence.

  4. For fixed bounded Z with mean zero and u C³ near w, uniform Taylor expansion gives E[u(w+εZ)]−u(w)=u″(w)ε²E[Z²]/2+O(|ε|³). The CE converges to w by continuity and strict local monotonicity. Since u′ stays positively bounded nearby, the mean-value theorem gives CE−w=O(ε²). Expanding u(CE) then gives u′(w)(CE−w)=u″(w)ε²E[Z²]/2+O(|ε|³), which yields the premium formula. Its constants are tied to this fixed shock and neighborhood.

    For log wealth 10±3ε, multiply the two outcomes to obtain CE=s=√(100−9ε²). Rationalization gives 10−s=9ε²/(10+s). Subtracting 9ε²/20 and rationalizing 10−s again yields 81ε⁴/[20(10+s)²]. At ε=1/2, s=√391/2>9, so the error is positive and less than 81/[320·19²]=81/115520<1/1000. The approximate premium is 9/80 and the exact premium is 10−√391/2. The tighter O(ε⁴) expression here arises from this symmetric explicit log case; it is not inferred from the generic C³ hypotheses.

  5. Write each u(xj) as u(x₁) plus the preceding increments. The expectation difference of the constant vanishes; the coefficient of increment k is Pr(X>xk)−Pr(Y>xk)=FY(xk)−FX(xk). This proves the summation identity. Nonnegative increments give the value inequality under the CDF order. Conversely test increasing indicators 1{x>xk} to recover every CDF inequality. Constancy between union knots completes the all-threshold argument.

    At (1,2,4,5), A’s masses are (0,1/2,0,1/2), B’s are (1/2,0,1/2,0), and FA−FB is (−1/2,0,−1/2,0). Therefore A≽₁B. Every strictly increasing u has positive increments where at least one CDF gap is positive, giving strict expected preference; a constant u ties. Means 7/2 and 5/2 differ, so a conditional-mean coupling and therefore a mean-preserving spread are impossible, despite the first- and second-order dominance.

  6. Necessity of LX≤LY uses ut(x)=−(t−x)+, increasing and concave. For sufficiency, thresholds above both supports imply E[X]≥E[Y]. Interpolate any increasing concave utility on the union support. Its nonnegative decreasing slopes give the affine-plus-negative-hinges decomposition in Section 3, so its expectation difference is a nonnegative mean term minus nonnegative multiples of LX−LY. The order follows, with the one- and two-point cases reducing to constants or affine terms. Piecewise linearity means all-real-threshold verification reduces to union knots. If E[Y|X]=X, iterated expectation gives equal means and conditional Jensen gives the concave order.

    For the converse under equal means, min(x,min y) excludes X below the Y interval; min(x,max y) excludes X above it because truncating that mass would lower its expectation below Y’s. If Y is constant, X must coincide. Otherwise conditional distributions on Y with each mean xi exist using endpoints. Their attainable column marginals form a nonempty compact convex K. If q is outside, closest-point separation gives h·q>maxr∈Kh·r. Let H(x) maximize the h payoff among distributions on Y of mean x. Mixing proves concavity; optimality and a mass/mean-preserving perturbation reduce an optimum to at most two positive weights. Thus H is a continuous finite piecewise-affine upper boundary with finite slopes, and some H+Mx is increasing concave. Equal means let the M terms cancel, so the assumed order gives E[H(X)]≥E[H(Y)]≥h·q. But independent row optimization makes maxr∈Kh·r=E[H(X)], the contradiction. Therefore the desired marginal is attainable and γij=piwij constructs the coupling.

    For sure X=3 and Y=1 or 5 equally, E[Y|X]=3, so this is a spread and X≽₂Y. At t=1 the CDF of X is 0 and that of Y is 1/2; at t=3 the order reverses to 1 versus 1/2. Hence no FSD. Utility min(x,3) gives 3 versus 2, and linear utility gives equal values 3, illustrating weak rather than universal strict preference.

  7. The second moments are 6 and 7; subtracting the common mean square 4 gives variances 2 and 3. On (0,1,3,5), FX=(1/3,1/3,1,1) and FY=(0,3/4,3/4,1); their differences are (1/3,−5/12,1/4,0), ruling out FSD in either direction. LX=(0,1/3,1,3) and LY=(0,0,3/2,3), so the differences (0,1/3,−1/2,0) also rule out SSD in both directions. The capped utility min(x,1) gives 2/3 versus 1, preferring Y, while min(x,3) gives 2 versus 3/2, preferring X. Adding εx for any ε>0 yields strictly increasing concave witnesses with the same strict rankings, because both means are 2. The variance ranking therefore cannot establish the colleague’s universal claim.

  8. The joint probabilities of H,+ and L,+ are 1/4 and 1/6, summing to 5/12; posterior H is 3/5. For − they are 1/12 and 1/2, summing to 7/12; posterior H is 1/7. Investment’s posterior means are 6(3/5)−3(2/5)=12/5 and 6/7−18/7=−12/7. The safe action is always zero. Thus V(P)=(5/12)(12/5)=1, V₀=max(0,2−2)=0 and V*=(1/3)6=2. A certain nonnegative fee c is worthwhile relative to no information iff 1−c≥0, with a tie at c=1.

    For any finite experiment, a prior-optimal action a* yields the decomposition V−V₀=Σqs[maxaβ(s)·Ua−β(s)·Ua*]. Every term is nonnegative, so equality is equivalent to a* being posterior-optimal at every positive-probability signal; conversely any common optimum attains both values. With payoff (6,0), investment is a common optimum and both values equal 2. Under a concave wealth utility a money fee belongs inside u(w+payoff−c); subtracting c from expected utility confuses wealth and utility units and generally changes preferences incorrectly.

  9. Multiplication gives Q=((7/12,5/12),(5/12,7/12)). Signal probabilities are 17/36 and 19/36, and H posteriors are 7/17 and 5/19. Investment’s posterior values are 12/17 and −12/19; invest only after + to obtain V(Q)=1/3. Under P, invest with probabilities 2/3 after + and 1/3 after −. The unnormalized P investment contributions are 1 and −1, so this randomized policy earns (2/3)1+(1/3)(−1)=1/3. It exactly simulates Q, while direct P optimization earns 1.

    Q’s determinant is 1/6, so a putative K with QK=P must equal Q⁻¹P=((2,−1),(−1,2)); its negative entries rule out a garbling. With a 3/4 fee, P nets 1/4 and loses to free Q’s 1/3. In general P is weakly preferable at an extra fee d exactly when 1−d≥1/3, or d≤2/3. This acquisition comparison leaves the free-information theorem intact.

  10. If Q=PG, simulate any Q rule D by GD under P. The statewise action distributions PGD=QD and thus every prior expected payoff agree. Maximization and the linearity argument for deterministic optimal actions give V(P)≥V(Q). Conversely the attainable set K={PG} is nonempty compact convex. If Q∉K, choose a nearest C∈K, set H=Q−C, and differentiate the squared distance along C+t(Z−C): ⟨H,Z−C⟩≤0. Therefore ⟨H,Q⟩=⟨H,C⟩+‖H‖²>maxZ∈K⟨H,Z⟩.

    Use ℓ actions, uniform prior 1/n and Uit=nHit. P’s feasible rules are exactly the garbling matrices G, so its value is the right-hand maximum. Under Q the identity rule earns the strictly larger left side. This is a finite payoff witness contradicting universal dominance. With any fixed πi>0 use Uit=Hit/πi instead. If π=(1,0), however, P=((1),(1)) and Q=I₂ give the same value maxaU1a for every payoff matrix, although every PG has equal rows and Q does not. Full support and all-payoff quantification cannot be replaced by a single observed decision.

  11. For job 1, E perfectly distinguishes state 1 and earns 1. H reveals state 2 with probability 1/3, when “not 1” is certainly right, and otherwise leaves an equal mixture of states 1 and 3, giving conditional success 1/2; its value is 1/3+(2/3)(1/2)=2/3. Exchange state labels 1 and 2 to obtain job-2 values (2/3,1). Thus each experiment is strictly better in one decision problem. Repeated-row preservation separately rules out E→H using rows 2,3 and H→E using rows 1,3.

    For three-state classification, each experiment identifies one state with probability 1/3 and leaves two equally likely states with probability 2/3, again giving value 2/3. Its singleton posterior has squared distance 2/3 from π; its two-state posterior has squared distance 1/6. Both posterior energies are therefore (1/3)(2/3)+(2/3)(1/6)=1/3. Equality on these summaries does not give equality of every decision value, and the two binary tasks explicitly refute such an inference. The conditional distributions, not just a summary statistic, are the objects in the garbling theorem.

  12. Illustrative recommendation. The reported accuracy and dispersion may be useful performance summaries for their specified population, but they do not prove Blackwell dominance. Use a common state definition and inspect whether a nonnegative row-stochastic garbling exactly relates the maintained experiments; if not, identify the relevant decision class rather than claiming a universal order. Specify users’ priors, available actions and when actions are chosen. Apply their cardinal utility to wealth consequences rather than treating money as utility without a risk-neutrality assumption. Compare net values with actual fees, budgets and timing; costless dominance does not ensure purchase is worthwhile, and ignored signals or randomized rules must truly be feasible. Estimated matrices require a sampling/measurement model and uncertainty assessment; neither a point estimate nor a synthetically exact calculation proves stability or transport to other populations. Case 6 supplies opposite-task witnesses despite equal classification and energy, while case 5 shows a dominated free experiment can beat a costly dominating one. A useful next test is a prespecified relevant payoff menu and acquisition cost together with a documented estimate of the full state-by-signal tables; it supports a conditional decision recommendation, with uncertainty stated, rather than a universal population claim.

    Scoring. Award 2 points for each of the six requested dimensions: 1 for the correct issue and 1 for an explicit hypothesis, calculation, witness or evidence design addressing it. A valid alternative witness or experiment earns equal credit. Vague calls for “more data” without a state/action or uncertainty contract earn at most 1 in that dimension. Full credit does not require recommending either vendor; it requires a justified scope of the recommendation. No empirical confidence level can be calculated from the supplied statements because no sampling law or sample is supplied.

8. Teach-back, retention and reproducibility

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why the phrase “less uncertainty” does not identify a purchase decision. A complete answer names a preference index over consequences, a distribution or experiment order, an action problem and the acquisition contract. Use case 3 to show that lower variance need not satisfy every risk-averse utility, and case 5 to show that a free-information order can coexist with a reversed net-fee decision. The common thread is that a universal inequality carries a specified domain and unchanged opportunities.

Delayed retention. Without looking back, answer: (i) if P costs 3/4 and Q is free in case 5, what are their net values and does the purchase ranking refute Blackwell? (ii) can equality of all values under prior (1,0) establish two-state experiment equivalence? Answers: (i) 1/4 and 1/3, so choose Q; the free garbling order remains true. (ii) No: the constant signal and full revelation agree at that degenerate prior although their second rows cannot be reconstructed by garbling. A full-support prior and all finite payoff matrices are sufficient in the proved theorem.

Reproduce the finite evidence. For any experiment in the cases, form the joint table πiPis, divide positive column sums for posteriors, and maximize the joint weighted payoff separately in each column. Independently enumerate every deterministic signal-to-action map and compare its largest total. For dominance, compute CDFs and E[(t−X)+] at the union support, then check the opposing capped-utility witnesses. These finite procedures reproduce every numerical comparison without a statistical package. Editorial numerical checks follow these independent routes and reject malformed probability tables; they support the displayed calculations but do not replace the universal proofs above.

9. Source and extension boundaries

The author inspected the scoped substantive text of the three linked MIT 2015 chapters and eight selected equation-page images. Börgers’s 2023 notes were inspected through the actual web-extracted text on pages 1–7; direct PDF retrieval returned HTTP 403, and no retained PDF or viewed equation image is claimed for that source. No original Blackwell paper, unlisted source section or source problem set is claimed as read. The chapter’s proofs, lotteries, payoff matrices and exercises are original; source support and independent proof checking are distinct evidence.

The results here concern finite lotteries or explicitly assumed interval utilities, finite state/signal/action experiments, exact supplied probabilities and unchanged feasible action rules. Arbitrary measurable experiments, subjective probability axioms, ambiguity preferences, statistical comparison of estimated experiments and strategic information design require additional hypotheses and theory. A next study can ask which finite constructions survive limits and which decision rules remain measurable; none of those extensions is silently included in the finite theorem.

Next. General equilibrium and existence moves from individual decision problems to mutually consistent choices across markets. The compactness and separation reasoning here will help distinguish a feasible allocation or a supporting certificate from an equilibrium-existence proof, which requires additional fixed-point tools and economic hypotheses.
